Summary The Blockchain for Impact Funding Evidence Map will show what blockchain-based impact projects aim to do, how they are delivered, how far they progress after the pilot stage, and how strong the evidence is behind their results.2 Before committing to a full map of 800+ use cases, Metagov will run a four-week pilot on up to 30 publicly documented use cases. The pilot has two jobs: to test whether the method works, and to give GSR the information it needs to decide whether the full exercise is worth doing. The design follows the evidence and gap map (EGM) standards of the Campbell Collaboration and 3ie as closely as the setting allows.34 It differs from a conventional EGM in three disclosed ways, each justified below. First, cases are drawn from four partner portfolios rather than from a full literature search. Second, the map includes all levels of evidence, not just impact

ways, each justified below. First, cases are drawn from four partner portfolios rather than from a full literature search. Second, the map includes all levels of evidence, not just impact evaluations, because a map restricted to impact evaluations would be almost empty in this field. Third, two LLMs from different developers act as independent coders, with a third model suggesting resolutions to disagreements and the human researcher making every final decision. Key design features: • Unit of analysis: the use case, meaning one solution applied to one problem in one setting. Each use case is linked to multiple documents and has a lineage ID to prevent double counting across portfolios. • Sample: 30 public use cases from four portfolios (11 MCV, 11 UNICEF, 5 Filecoin and 3 GSR, after places that Filecoin and GSR could not fill were reallocated). Cases are chosen by stratified purposive selection with random draws inside strata, and stalled and discontinued cases are deliberately included. • Framework: a matrix of six use-case domains by six outcome

Each one is built into the pilot, and their usefulness is reviewed at G5. 1. Grade what exists rather than exclude it. An inclusive five-level scale replaces impact-evaluation-only inclusion, so thin evidence becomes visible as a gap rather than disappearing. 2. Grade each outcome separately. A use case can have L3 evidence on cost and L1 on wellbeing. A single grade per case would hide this. 3. Separate “not reported” from “not applicable”. Every field allows both codes, so missing evidence is never confused with evidence of no effect. 4. Code who produced the evidence. The codes are self-reported by the

“not applicable”. Every field allows both codes, so missing evidence is never confused with evidence of no effect. 4. Code who produced the evidence. The codes are self-reported by the implementer, partner or funder, independent, or peer-reviewed. Most material will come from parties with an interest in positive results, so this filter lets readers see the map with self-reported evidence removed. 5. Check claims against what happened next. Headline claims, such as a 75% cost reduction, are logged in a claims register and checked against later sources and post-pilot status. This tests the memo’s question of whether pilots are inflating utility.29 6. Trace post-pilot status from digital signals. Signals include whether the product is live, the latest public activity, follow-on funding, hand-over announcements and, where relevant, on-chain or code-repository activity. Each is coded with a confidence level. 7. Treat on-chain data as operational evidence only. Transaction records can verify usage and speed, but not social outcomes. The codebook caps on-chain evidence at L2 unless it is linked to outcome data.

General rules: These rules apply to every field. - **R1 Evidence only from the packet.** Code only from the evidence packet. Do not use outside knowledge, even if you believe it is correct. - **R2 Quote and source for every code.** Every code other than "not reported" or "not applicable" needs a source ID (for example S01) and a verbatim quote. The quote must be copied character for character from one source and be 300 characters or fewer. Use the shortest span that supports the code. Do not join text from different places. - **R3 Not reported versus not applicable.** - Use "not reported" when the field applies but the packet says nothing about it. - Use "not applicable" only when the field cannot apply (for example, a cash-transfer case has no "children" population unless the sources name one). - Never treat silence as evidence of no effect. - **R4 Confidence for every code.** - High: the source states the code directly. - Medium: the code needs a short, clear inference. -

General rules: silence as evidence of no effect. - **R4 Confidence for every code.** - High: the source states the code directly. - Medium: the code needs a short, clear inference. - Low: the code needs a judgement between plausible options. Low-confidence codes go to human review. - **R5 Insufficient information.** List a field in `insufficient_information` only when the packet has relevant evidence but it does not let you choose between options. Use this instead of guessing. Do not list fields coded "not reported". - **R6 Sources disagree.** Code the figure or statement from the most specific source: an endline report is more specific than a summary page, which is more specific than a promotional page. Record the conflict in the claims fields (field 17). - **R7 Funder text.** Partner or funder pages are evidence produced by the partner or funder (field 12). They are not independent evidence, even when written in a neutral tone.
Fields: The orchestrator pre-fills the identification fields from the sampling frame (O2). Coders do not code them: case ID, lineage ID, organisation ID, name, primary portfolio and all funders.

Purpose and Use Memo: Blockchain for Impact Funding Evidence Map To: GSR Foundation From: Michael Cooper, Research Director, Metagov (mike@metagov.org · Telegram: MCooperResearch) Please note: Everything in this memo is a draft and needs GSR's validation. It is based on GSR's initial answers about purpose, audience and success, and on GSR's public website. Proposed targets and design choices are suggestions, not commitments. The full Evidence Map depends on the outcome of a four-week pilot, described in Section 8. The final section lists the questions we need GSR to answer before the memo can be finalised. 1. Purpose This memo records who the Blockchain for Impact Funding Evidence Map is for, what decisions it should inform, and how we will judge whether it was useful. Once agreed, it becomes the reference point for design choices and for each partner review milestone. If a proposed piece of work does not serve the uses below, we will drop it or raise it with GSR. 2. What the Evidence Map is The Blockchain for

If a proposed piece of work does not serve the uses below, we will drop it or raise it with GSR. 2. What the Evidence Map is The Blockchain for Impact Funding Evidence Map is a structured, public overview of blockchain-based impact projects supported by GSR and its partners. For each project, it records what the project set out to achieve, how it was delivered, what happened after the pilot, and how strong the evidence is behind its reported results. It will show both where evidence exists and where it is missing. The Evidence Map is designed to answer the following draft research questions: 1. What objectives are blockchain-based impact projects pursuing, and in which sectors and countries?

2. What implementation models do they use, including who delivers them, which blockchain features they rely on, and how they are funded? 3. How far do projects advance? Which ones never move beyond the pilot stage, and which are extended, scaled, handed over or shut down? 4. What is the quality of the evidence available on their performance? Does it cover only operational measures such as speed and cost, or does it include data on social outcomes? 5. How well did projects achieve their stated objectives, based on the available evidence? 6. Does any evidence show that blockchain added value compared with simpler, nonblockchain alternatives? 7. Where is evidence weak or missing, and which gaps matter most for funding decisions? The unit of analysis is the use case, meaning one solution applied to one problem in one setting. Each use case will be classified by its objective, implementation model, blockchain function, deployment status and evidence grade, and by how well it achieved its objectives. The results will be presented as a matrix of use-case categories against outcomes, supported by a short report. The categories, definitions and grading rules will be finalized in the taxonomy developed during the pilot (Section 8). 3.
